idiom_name: overloaded methods on tag classes, plus Class<T> runtime type tokens when the type must travel
implementation_notes: Java performs overload resolution at compile time, so a final marker class per branch plus a set of overloaded methods reproduces the literal pattern for a closed set: the tag is a compile-time marker and the caller's static types select the method. The generic form is impossible: generics are erased, type variables do not exist at run time, and a generic class is shared by all its invocations, so there is no per-instantiation class to dispatch on and no way to rank overloads on a type parameter. What replaces the classic structure: hand-written tag overloads for closed sets, and when the type must be carried past the call site, a Class<T> token (the runtime-type-token idiom the JDK itself uses, e.g. Class<T>.newInstance and annotation APIs) with a runtime comparison inside - i.e. the decision moves to run time. The classic form is justified when the caller knows the concrete type; otherwise a Strategy object with an interface is the Java-idiomatic answer.
pitfalls: Erasure makes overloads that differ only in a type argument identical after erasure, so such pairs do not compile (or are silently glued by compiler-generated bridge methods) - the ladder must be keyed on distinct runtime classes, not on List<Integer> versus List<String>.

A Class<T> token reintroduces exactly the runtime check the pattern removes, and its use is easy to hide inside utility code; the compile-time guarantee is gone the moment the type is expressed as a value.

getClass()/instanceof chains inside a generic method are neither exhaustive nor ordered by specificity the way an overload ladder is: the first matching if wins, and subclass relationships must be hand-ordered.
sources: Oracle, The Fine Print (Generics): 'Type variables don't exist at run time', a generic class is shared by all its invocations, https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/extra/generics/fineprint.html
Oracle, Class Literals as Runtime-Type Tokens (the Class<T> token idiom), https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/extra/generics/literals.html
Oracle, Effects of Type Erasure and Bridge Methods, https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/generics/bridgeMethods.html
